channel.title: Runix Blog
channel.description: Engineering notes on LLM gateways, reliability, cost control and data pipelines, from the team building Runix.

item.title: DPO fine-tuning explained: what preference tuning changes and what it cannot
item.description: How DPO fine-tuning learns from chosen and rejected pairs without a reward model, where preference tuning helps and where it cannot, and the data pitfalls.

item.title: The harness: what actually runs an AI agent
item.description: An agent harness is the runtime around a model: tools, permissions, context, budgets and logs. Why it, not the model, decides if an agent is safe to run.

item.title: Single-tenant model serving explained: what a dedicated LLM inference endpoint changes
item.description: What single-tenant serving means beside a shared endpoint: isolation, latency under your own load, capacity planning, quantised variants and operations.

item.title: Fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompting: a decision guide by failure mode
item.description: When a prompt is enough, when retrieval fixes a knowledge or freshness gap, when fine-tuning is the right tool, and how the failure mode tells you which one.

item.title: Keeping GPUs fed: where the GPU data loading bottleneck comes from
item.description: How input pipelines starve accelerators: dataloader workers, random reads, IOPS versus throughput, object storage latency, and honest utilisation metrics.

item.title: Split by source, not by row: how benchmark contamination reaches your own evaluation set
item.description: Row splits put near-duplicates on both sides of an evaluation. Why to split by repository, document or entity, and how to decontaminate and report overlap.

item.title: LoRA vs QLoRA vs full fine-tuning: what each one changes in the weights
item.description: What LoRA and QLoRA change in the weights, the memory and quality trade-offs, merging versus adapter serving, and when full fine-tuning is still warranted.

item.title: Reviewable by default: why an agent's changes should land as diffs
item.description: Agent output should land as a diff a person can review, not a silent write. Blast radius, attribution, tests as the gate, and how reviewing an agent differs.

item.title: A multi-tier cache for AI training data: what goes where
item.description: Memory, SSD and HDD tiers for training data: what goes where, how eviction and warming work, page cache or distributed cache, and when caching is pointless.

item.title: Fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests in clean containers: what makes a coding task valid
item.description: Fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests, clean containers, why a task whose tests pass without the patch is invalid, and what SWE-bench Verified screened for.

item.title: FUSE, CSI or SDK: three ways to mount object storage in Kubernetes for ML workloads
item.description: FUSE mount, CSI driver or SDK: three ways to get a bucket into ML pods on Kubernetes, what each changes in your code, how each fails, and when to pick which.

item.title: How to read an open-weight model licence before you fine-tune it
item.description: The clauses that decide whether you can fine-tune and ship an open-weight model: use restrictions, attribution, user thresholds, redistribution and patents.

item.title: How to read an LLM price list
item.description: Units, cached input, batch and tiered rates, context bands and media pricing: how to read a vendor's LLM price list and record a dated baseline to compare on.

item.title: How to evaluate a fine-tuned LLM against the model you run today
item.description: Held-out sets, task metrics versus generic benchmarks, regression checks on what you did not tune, contamination, and when a tuned model is ready to ship.

item.title: What is a coding agent? From autocomplete to pull requests
item.description: A coding agent reads a repository, plans, edits files, runs tests and revises until they pass. What separates it from an assistant, and what it is not.

item.title: Why five layers: how Runix drew its AI infrastructure stack
item.description: How Runix drew five layers over the customer's own compute, which Unix idea each layer rebuilds, why each must work alone, and what the layered view omits.

item.title: PII masking for training data that fails closed: detect, mask, measure, hold back
item.description: Pattern, NER and context detection, masking versus pseudonymisation versus dropping, why uncleared records are held back, and how to measure recall honestly.

item.title: The small files problem in machine learning: millions of samples, one metadata bill
item.description: Why millions of small samples cost more than their bytes: per-object overhead, listing, metadata pressure, and packing formats versus a metadata service.

item.title: Exact, near and semantic: why near-duplicate detection for training data needs all three
item.description: Exact hashing, MinHash and embeddings each catch a different kind of duplicate. What each misses and costs, and how duplicates inflate evaluation scores.

item.title: Auto routing versus a pinned model id: choosing an LLM routing policy
item.description: Two routing policies behind one endpoint: auto, chosen by cost and health, or a pinned model id. When each is right, and what to log to keep both honest.

item.title: When the bucket is the truth: AI file system cache mode versus file-system mode
item.description: Cache mode and fs mode: what each guarantees about the bucket behind an AI file system, which workloads fit which, and what to ask a vendor about truth.

item.title: Turning an LLM bill into a policy: budgets per team and per feature
item.description: Turning an LLM bill into enforceable policy: per-key quotas, allowed models, hard stops versus alerts, what happens at the limit, and how retries draw on it.

item.title: Training data provenance: what every record should carry, and why a README is not proof
item.description: What a provenance entry should carry per record, from source and retrieval date to an SPDX licence identifier, and why a detected licence beats a README.

item.title: Domain-specific AI agents: why agents are built one profession at a time
item.description: Why AI agents are built per profession: the domain supplies the tools, the data rules, the evaluation and the review gate, and a generic agent lacks all four.

item.title: Evaluate coding agents on your own repository, not on a leaderboard
item.description: Leaderboard scores do not transfer to your codebase. How to build a task set from closed issues with fail-to-pass tests, and what to measure beyond pass rate.

item.title: Object storage is not a file system, and what POSIX on object storage adds
item.description: Object storage has no rename, no partial writes and no directories. What a POSIX layer over a bucket has to add, and what it still cannot promise.

item.title: What a data quality report should contain, and how to read one sceptically
item.description: What a data quality report should state about coverage, duplication, extraction confidence, drops and licences, and how a buyer reads one sceptically.

item.title: Rebuild AI Unix: why Runix Lab is building an operating system for AI
item.description: Unix lasted on a few ideas: files, pipes, a kernel, one call interface. Runix Lab is rebuilding them for enterprise AI, in five layers.

item.title: Introducing Runix FS: an AI file system for object storage
item.description: Runix FS puts a POSIX file system and a multi-tier cache in front of object storage. Why the layer is missing, what it is built on, and how early access works.

item.title: One key can drain a shared quota pool
item.description: A shared quota pool with no per-key ceiling is first-come-first-served — one client's batch job empties it. Why runway beats balance as an alert threshold.

item.title: Why your LLM bill doesn't match the price list
item.description: Cache multipliers, injected prompts, tokenizer changes, tiered rates: the mechanics behind a surprising token bill, and how to reconcile one request by hand.

item.title: The security review an LLM gateway should survive
item.description: Eight questions a security review should ask any LLM gateway — key custody, logging, retention, tenant isolation, egress — and what good answers look like.

item.title: Your LLM traffic needs a retry budget, not a retry count
item.description: Retries multiply cost and load exactly when a provider is struggling. What a retry budget is, which errors deserve one, and how failover changes the arithmetic.

item.title: Where your prompts actually go
item.description: Every security review opens with this and most teams cannot answer it. How to trace the path text takes through an LLM integration, hop by hop.

item.title: How long should an LLM request be allowed to take?
item.description: Standard HTTP timeout advice is wrong for model traffic. Which timeout to set, where each one belongs, and why stacked timeouts cause the outage.

item.title: What to settle before an LLM feature carries real traffic
item.description: Twelve decisions that are cheap before launch and expensive after: cost ceilings, timeouts, failover, what you log, and how you roll back.

item.title: Your model id has an expiry date
item.description: Providers retire model versions on a published schedule. If the id is a string literal in your code, their calendar is your deploy calendar.

item.title: "OpenAI-compatible" is a surface, not a contract
item.description: Compatibility claims cover the endpoint shape, rarely the details that break you: ignored parameters, missing usage, streaming that ends wrong. How to test one.

item.title: How to tell whether a model change made things worse
item.description: Output varies run to run, so a quality regression does not announce itself. Four signals that move before anyone files a ticket.

item.title: Migrating to a gateway without a maintenance window
item.description: Shadow, then a percentage, then a cutover you can reverse in one config change — and the three things about LLM traffic the usual playbook does not cover.

item.title: Comic Drama vs Webtoon vs Motion Comic, Explained
item.description: Three overlapping formats for drawn stories: how webtoons, motion comics and comic dramas differ in production, distribution and audience — and which to make.

item.title: How to Make a Comic Drama with AI: Script to Screen
item.description: The full AI comic drama production line: script and characters, storyboards, styled panels, motion, voice and publishing — and where tools still fall short.

item.title: LLM Router vs LLM Gateway: What's the Difference?
item.description: The two names describe overlapping tools. What routing and gateway features actually do, when the difference matters, and how to choose on capabilities.

item.title: OpenRouter Alternatives: A Buyer's Checklist
item.description: Evaluating LLM gateways beyond routing: the contract, data, failover and cost-attribution questions that decide whether a gateway survives procurement.

item.title: What Is an LLM Gateway? A Plain Definition
item.description: An LLM gateway is a control plane between your application and model providers. What it does, what it does not do, and when a team actually needs one.

item.title: Surviving LLM Rate Limits: 429s, Budgets and Queues
item.description: Why provider rate limits bite in bursts, how RPM, TPM and concurrency interact, and the queueing and backoff patterns that keep throughput stable under 429s.

item.title: Streaming LLM Responses Without Breaking Failover
item.description: Once tokens have reached the user, failover stops being free. Mid-stream failure modes, what a proxy must preserve, and how to degrade without duplicating text.

item.title: What to Log for LLM Traffic, and What Not To
item.description: Status codes and latency miss the failures that matter for LLM traffic. The signals worth recording, the fields to redact, and the alerts worth waking up for.

item.title: LLM Provider Keys: Scope, Rotation and Blast Radius
item.description: Provider keys spread through repos, CI and notebooks. How to scope and rotate them, and why a compromised LLM key is a billing incident as well as a data one.

item.title: Per-Team LLM Cost Attribution That Survives Audit
item.description: Provider invoices arrive as one number. How to attach cost to a team, feature and request at call time, and why reconstructing it later never works.

item.title: Prompt Caching: When It Pays and When It Bites
item.description: How provider-side prompt caching works, the prefix rule that decides whether you get hits, and the cases where caching quietly changes behaviour.

item.title: 12 Data Questions to Ask an AI Vendor
item.description: The data-handling questions that decide an AI procurement review, what a good answer sounds like, and which vague replies should stop the process.

item.title: Build or Buy an LLM Gateway: An Honest Comparison
item.description: The first version of a gateway is a weekend. The parts that take a year are retry budgets, streaming failover, cost accounting and being on call for all of it.

item.title: LLM Cost Control: Tokens, Caching, and Budgets Explained
item.description: Token pricing asymmetry, prompt caching, model routing, budgets and kill switches — and the waste patterns that quietly inflate an LLM bill.

item.title: From Raw to Model-Ready: A Practical Guide to AI Data Pipelines
item.description: A stage-by-stage guide to AI data pipelines: ingestion, cleaning, deduplication, LLM-powered extraction, PII masking and quality scoring.

item.title: Designing for Model Failover: Lessons from Production LLM Traffic
item.description: Keeping LLM-backed products up when providers degrade: failure taxonomy, retry budgets, circuit breakers, failover trade-offs and degradation tiers.

item.title: Choosing an LLM Gateway: Seven Things That Actually Matter
item.description: How to evaluate an LLM gateway: API compatibility, failover behaviour, rate limits, cost tracking, observability, security and operational burden.

item.title: Introducing Runix
item.description: Why we started Runix and what we set out to build: the gateway now called Runix Router, the pipelines now Runix Pipeline and Runix Data, and what came next.
